detailed_findings.finding: Claim 2 uses the implication g(n) >= n^(α-ε) => g(n)^(α-ε) >= n^((α-ε)^2) without ensuring α-ε >= 0. For ε > α, the power is negative and the inequality reverses, so the step is invalid as written.
A simple fix is available: since g is strictly increasing and integer-valued, g(n) >= n for n>=1, hence α >= 1. Restrict ε to 0<ε<1 (or 0<ε<α) before the exponentiation step.
The proof ignores hypothesis (ii), but this is acceptable because it proves a stronger nonexistence statement from (i) alone.

feedback_for_solver: Repair Claim 2 explicitly: after proving g(n) >= n for all n>1, record α = liminf log g(n)/log n >= 1. Then in Claim 2 take 0<ε<1 (hence α-ε>0), not arbitrary ε. With α-ε>0, from g(n) >= n^(α-ε) you may legitimately raise both sides to the power α-ε to get g(n)^(α-ε) >= n^((α-ε)^2). The rest of the summation/liminf argument then goes through unchanged, and letting ε -> 0 yields α >= 1 + r α^2.
reason: The argument is essentially the standard liminf-growth contradiction and appears mathematically sound overall, but Claim 2 as written has a local gap: it fixes arbitrary ε>0 and then uses g(n) >= n^(α-ε) to infer g(n)^(α-ε) >= n^((α-ε)^2), which is only monotone in the needed direction when α-ε >= 0. This is easily repaired by first noting α >= 1 from g(n) >= n, and then restricting to 0<ε<α (or just 0<ε<1), which is sufficient since only ε -> 0 is needed.
